questions.question: At 1 minute of life a newborn has a heart rate of 120 beats per minute, irregular respiratory effort, some flexion of the limbs, a weak cry, and a pre-ductal SpO2 of 62%. What should the nurse do next?

Perform chest compressions and intubate
Dry the newborn, provide warmth, and reassess after 30 seconds
questions.explanation: The keyed answer. Because the baby is breathing with a heart rate above 100 but has laboured, irregular respiration, the response is to attach the pulse oximeter to the right hand and titrate oxygen against the minute-by-minute targets rather than to ventilate. Note that the targeted pre-ductal saturation at 1 minute is only 60 to 65 per cent, so a reading of 62 per cent is already within range and oxygen should be given only if the saturation falls below target on continued monitoring.

explanations.A: Positive-pressure ventilation is triggered by apnoea, gasping or a heart rate below 100 beats per minute. This baby is breathing and the heart rate is 120, so PPV is not indicated.
explanations.B: The keyed answer. Because the baby is breathing with a heart rate above 100 but has laboured, irregular respiration, the response is to attach the pulse oximeter to the right hand and titrate oxygen against the minute-by-minute targets rather than to ventilate. Note that the targeted pre-ductal saturation at 1 minute is only 60 to 65 per cent, so a reading of 62 per cent is already within range and oxygen should be given only if the saturation falls below target on continued monitoring.
explanations.C: Chest compressions are started only when the heart rate stays below 60 beats per minute after 30 seconds of effective ventilation with a secured airway. Nothing here justifies them.
explanations.D: Warmth, drying and stimulation are the initial steps completed within the first 30 seconds; by 1 minute they have been done, and management now turns on the ongoing assessment of breathing, heart rate and saturation.

questions.explanation: This is classic infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. It declares itself between 3 and 8 weeks of age, more often in first-born males, with non-bilious projectile vomiting, an insatiable appetite immediately afterwards, weight loss and the palpable pyloric 'olive'. The obstruction is above the ampulla, so the vomit contains no bile, and loss of gastric acid produces a hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis that must be corrected before pyloromyotomy. Ultrasound confirms the thickened elongated pylorus.

explanations.A: Reflux produces effortless posseting or regurgitation soon after feeds, usually in a thriving baby. It never produces a palpable olive or visible gastric peristalsis.
explanations.B: Intussusception typically strikes between 6 and 18 months with paroxysmal colic, drawing up of the legs, a sausage-shaped mass and redcurrant-jelly stools, and the vomiting turns bilious rather than remaining non-bilious.
explanations.C: This is classic infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. It declares itself between 3 and 8 weeks of age, more often in first-born males, with non-bilious projectile vomiting, an insatiable appetite immediately afterwards, weight loss and the palpable pyloric 'olive'. The obstruction is above the ampulla, so the vomit contains no bile, and loss of gastric acid produces a hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis that must be corrected before pyloromyotomy. Ultrasound confirms the thickened elongated pylorus.
explanations.D: Duodenal atresia presents within the first day or two of life with bilious vomiting and the 'double bubble' sign on abdominal X-ray, and it is strongly associated with Down syndrome.

questions.question: Light-headedness and one episode of almost blacking out bring a 65-year-old man to the emergency department. He has had diabetes mellitus for years and is known to have coronary artery disease. His monitor shows a slow rhythm made up of broad QRS complexes. Which intervention should the nurse anticipate as the most appropriate?
options: Amiodarone
Transcutaneous pacemaker insertion
Anticoagulant therapy with continuous observation
Atropine
questions.explanation: A bradycardia that is producing symptoms of poor perfusion, such as near-syncope, and that carries a wide QRS suggesting block below the AV node, is an indication to capture the heart electrically. Transcutaneous pacing restores an adequate rate immediately while definitive therapy is arranged.

explanations.A: Amiodarone belongs to the tachyarrhythmia toolkit. Given to a patient who is already too slow, it depresses conduction further and can push the rate down towards asystole.
explanations.B: A bradycardia that is producing symptoms of poor perfusion, such as near-syncope, and that carries a wide QRS suggesting block below the AV node, is an indication to capture the heart electrically. Transcutaneous pacing restores an adequate rate immediately while definitive therapy is arranged.
explanations.C: Anticoagulation lowers clot risk but does nothing about a failing conduction system, and simply watching a patient who is already fainting allows the rhythm to deteriorate before help is given.
explanations.D: Atropine is the opening drug in symptomatic bradycardia, yet its vagolytic action works at the AV node. In high-grade, infranodal block with wide complexes it usually fails, so the algorithm moves on to pacing.

questions.question: Parents are being prepared to take home an infant who is fed through a jejunostomy tube. Which point should the nurse stress in the discharge teaching?
options: Administer high-calorie formula orally to promote weight gain
Monitor the jejunostomy site daily for signs of infection or leakage
Clean the jejunostomy tube with alcohol-based solution twice daily
Restrict fluid intake to prevent excessive output from the jejunostomy
questions.explanation: Daily inspection of the exit site is the cornerstone of home care. Parents are taught to look for redness, swelling, warmth, discharge, excoriated skin, granulation tissue and leakage of feed around the tube, to keep the site clean and dry, to check the external marking so displacement is recognised, and to report any of these promptly. Leaking jejunal contents rapidly erode the surrounding skin, and a dislodged tube is an emergency because the tract closes quickly.

explanations.A: A jejunostomy is placed precisely because the oral or gastric route is unsafe or inadequate. Nutrition goes through the tube, usually as a continuous or slow intermittent infusion since the jejunum cannot handle bolus volumes; any oral intake is introduced only on the team's advice.
explanations.B: Daily inspection of the exit site is the cornerstone of home care. Parents are taught to look for redness, swelling, warmth, discharge, excoriated skin, granulation tissue and leakage of feed around the tube, to keep the site clean and dry, to check the external marking so displacement is recognised, and to report any of these promptly. Leaking jejunal contents rapidly erode the surrounding skin, and a dislodged tube is an emergency because the tract closes quickly.
explanations.C: Alcohol dehydrates and irritates peristomal skin and can degrade the tube material. Mild soap and water, dried well, is the recommended routine.
explanations.D: Withholding fluid in an infant on jejunal feeding invites dehydration and electrolyte disturbance. High output is managed by adjusting the rate, concentration or formula composition, and by replacing losses, not by limiting what the child receives.

questions.question: A newborn with myelomeningocele is kept under close watch for a rise in intracranial pressure. Which change at the anterior fontanelle would support that suspicion?

Normal fontanelle
Bulging fontanelle
Closed fontanelle
questions.explanation: Most babies with myelomeningocele develop hydrocephalus, frequently on the basis of an associated Arnold-Chiari II malformation. explanations.B: A soft, flat fontanelle that pulsates normally when the baby is quiet and upright is a reassuring finding and argues against raised pressure.
